# Papaya — Coding Agents for DevSecOps: Big-Tech Models & Top 3 Solutions > Role: Principal DevSecOps · Version: **v2 (revised)** · Date: 2026-11-05 > Method: 5 research sub-agents (3× Sonnet, 2× Haiku) → orchestrator synthesis → 3 fact-check sub-agents against primary sources → revision. > Verification status of every non-obvious claim is in [Appendix B](#appendix-b--verification-status). Remaining ⚠️ items are flagged inline. ### What changed in v2 - **HIPAA (material change):** Anthropic's BAA covers Claude Code on the **Enterprise** plan with HIPAA configuration enabled. The Team plan is not addressed, and Claude Code via Bedrock/Vertex is **explicitly not covered by Anthropic's BAA**. Bedrock's own coverage comes from the AWS BAA. This hardens the "agents never see PHI by default" rule and adds a Phase-0 legal gate. - **AWS TEAM corrected:** approval happens in the TEAM web app (Slack is notification-only), and there is no conditional auto-approval such as "on-call + incident". Solution 2's broker choice is updated accordingly. - **Multi-cloud coverage added:** GCP (Vertex AI), k0s, and Firebase Hosting were missing in v1. - **Added:** a weighted decision matrix, a compliance mapping (ISO 27001:2022 Annex A + HIPAA 164.312), a verified Claude Code managed-settings baseline, and CI prompt-injection risks for Solution 3. - **Corrected details:** CrossGuard has 4 enforcement levels, Serverless has no built-in diff, the AWS MCP condition key types, and the OWASP ASI titles. --- ## 0. Diagnosis: Papaya's actual problem | # | Current state | Risk | Applicable framework | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Laptop SSO profile reaches prod, and the agent inherits it | The agent acts as an engineer with prod rights. A prompt injection or a bad command hits prod directly | Google Zero-Touch Prod; AWS "read-only default + JIT" | | 2 | Permission prompts are turned off | No deterministic control between the model and the shell | OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency; Claude Code managed settings | | 3 | MCP servers and plugins are unreviewed | Supply chain, tool poisoning, credential theft | OWASP LLM03 / ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain; MCP security best practices | | 4 | Long-lived GitHub token and AWS keys in CI secrets | One leak gives persistent, unattributed access | Microsoft SFI; OIDC / Workload Identity Federation | | 5 | Monitoring is fragmented and on-call is informal | No evidence for ISO A.8.15/A.8.16 or HIPAA 164.312(b); slow detection | Central audit; Google "observable actions" | | 6 | Production AI agents read partner and member documents | Untrusted input combined with PHI and the ability to change claim state invites prompt injection | Meta "Agents Rule of Two"; lethal trifecta | | 7 | Coding agents may read PHI (prod logs, DB) and send it to the model provider | HIPAA exposure if the plan or channel isn't covered by a BAA | Anthropic BAA scope; AWS BAA for Bedrock | **Key point:** the conflict between Engineering and Compliance is not a dilemma. All the big-tech models below resolve it the same way: > **Agents and humans get broad freedom to *propose* and *observe*; only an attributable pipeline or broker *executes* changes on prod, after a named person approves.** Engineering gets speed: the agent writes the IaC, runs the preview, debugs read-only, and ships to dev and staging on its own. Compliance gets "a named person who reviewed and approved it" for every prod change. The design problem is making that approval step **fast** and **hard to bypass**. --- ## 1. Top 5 models used at large organizations ### Model 1 — Google: Zero-Touch Prod + Multi-Party Authorization (BeyondProd / BAB) - **Core idea:** no human holds standing access to prod. Every change goes through automation or small, safe APIs. Sensitive actions need a second person's approval (MPA). Code reaches prod only if it was reviewed and built on an isolated system with provenance (Binary Authorization for Borg). - **Key controls:** - Risk tiering: infra access is always high risk. - MPA on *specific actions*, not broad group grants. - A proxy for commands that lack fine-grained APIs. - Break-glass that is monitored, tested regularly and peer-reviewed every week. - Logs that carry a justification (ticket ID). - **Agent guidance** (Google's paper on secure AI agents): every agent has a clear *human controller*, *limited powers*, and *observable* actions and plans. - **Transferable:** - Default-deny for prod writes. - The agent goes through a narrow tool (plan, apply, deploy) instead of a raw shell or the AWS CLI. - Link each agent run to its approver and its change. - **Not worth it at Papaya's scale:** full ZTP, a self-built BAB, hardware trust, and service-mesh mTLS everywhere. - **Sources:** [BSRS ch.5](https://google.github.io/building-secure-and-reliable-systems/raw/ch05.html) · [BAB](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/binary-authorization-for-borg) · [Google secure AI agents](https://research.google/pubs/an-introduction-to-googles-approach-for-secure-ai-agents/) · [SAIF agent self-assessment](https://saif.google/agent-risk-self-assessment) ### Model 2 — Amazon/AWS: "Humans don't deploy, pipelines do" + read-only default + JIT - **Core idea:** code review is the last manual gate. Pipelines deploy in waves (one-box → AZ → region), with bake time and automatic rollback on alarm. People get **read-only by default**, and writes go through JIT: request, approval, then expiry. - **Key controls:** - IAM Identity Center permission sets. - [TEAM](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-identity-center-team): - Approvers are Identity Center groups scoped by account or OU, and self-approval is blocked. - Maximum duration is set per policy (1–8000h). - Each policy has an "Approval required" toggle. - **Approval happens in the TEAM web app.** Slack is only a notification channel. - Approver ≠ requester, and a different person audits temporary permissions. - SCPs and permission boundaries as a backstop. - GitHub OIDC with a strict `sub` (e.g. `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:production`) instead of long-lived keys. - **For agents:** - The [Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix](https://aws.amazon.com/ai/security/agentic-ai-scoping-matrix/) puts a coding agent at **Scope 2: Prescribed Agency**. The agent proposes and a human approves, and enforcement lives outside the model (IAM, SCP, Cedar). - The IAM condition keys `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` (Bool) and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` (String, e.g. `aws-mcp.amazonaws.com`) let a policy tell agent traffic apart from human traffic. - **Limit:** they only apply to calls made through an AWS-managed MCP service. A local MCP server or a CLI call run by Claude Code looks like a direct human call. On laptops, separate roles and session tags are the real control. - **Transferable:** almost all of it. Papaya is AWS-primary, so this is the most "native" model. - **Sources:** [Hands-off deployments](https://builder.aws.com/content/3ErTKQOTKc5NIw031UePBPxTQ6I/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments) · [AG.SAD.4 JIT](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/devops-guidance/ag.sad.4-limit-human-access-with-just-in-time-access.html) · [TEAM docs](https://aws-samples.github.io/iam-identity-center-team/docs/overview/workflow.html) · [IAM condition keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html) · [GitHub OIDC](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc) ### Model 3 — Microsoft: SFI + PIM/JIT with approval + Enterprise Access Model + dedicated agent identities - **Core idea:** the Secure Future Initiative is secure by design, secure by default, and secure in operations. It removes long-lived secrets, isolates credentials across boundaries, and limits which package endpoints pipelines can reach. - **Privileged access:** - PIM activation requires approval, approvers cannot approve their own requests, and *service principals cannot approve*. Activation is time-bound. - The Enterprise Access Model separates the control, management and data planes, and a lower plane never controls a higher one. - **Agent identity (Entra Agent ID):** agents are a separate identity type. They can *never* hold high-privilege roles (Global Admin, Privileged Role Admin…). Permissions such as `RoleManagement.ReadWrite.All` are blocked, and even an admin cannot consent to them. - **Transferable:** "**an agent can never grant itself privileges**". - Enforce it with an SCP or permission boundary that denies `iam:*`, `organizations:*` and `sso:*` to every session tagged as an agent. - Map the planes: AWS Organizations and Identity Center are the control plane (agents never touch it), infra accounts are the management plane, and Aurora plus the claim-document S3 buckets are the data plane (PHI). - **Sources:** [SFI 07/2026](https://microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/10/securing-our-future-july-2026-progress-report-on-microsofts-secure-future-initiative) · [PIM approval](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-approval-workflow) · [Entra Agent ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/authorization-agent-id) ### Model 4 — GitOps + Policy-as-Code: "the PR is the only road to prod" (HashiCorp, GitLab, Spacelift/Pulumi ecosystem) - **Core idea:** plan on the PR, run the policy check, get human review, and apply after merge. The approval is the PR review by a named person, so the audit trail comes for free. - **Tooling:** - **Pulumi CrossGuard:** has 4 levels: `advisory`, `mandatory`, `remediate`, `disabled`. - `pulumi preview --policy-pack ` runs on the open-source CLI. - Server-side enforcement through policy groups, plus the ready-made packs, require a paid Pulumi Cloud edition. - **GitHub rulesets:** "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push", plus CODEOWNERS. - **GitHub Environments:** required reviewers (up to 6) plus **Prevent self-review**. - **Strengths:** cheap, quick to adopt, and direct evidence for ISO 27001 A.8.32 Change management. - **Weakness:** it only covers changes that go through git. Debugging, incidents and console click-ops fall outside it, and drift detection only detects; it cannot prevent. - **Sources:** [CrossGuard config](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/crossguard/configuration/) · [Pulumi policy editions](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/policy/) · [GitHub rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets) · [Environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/managing-workflow-runs-and-deployments/managing-deployments/managing-environments-for-deployment) ### Model 5 — Agent containment: Meta "Rule of Two" + GitHub Copilot coding-agent sandbox + OWASP Agentic Top 10 + Claude Code managed settings - **[Meta Agents Rule of Two](https://ai.meta.com/blog/practical-ai-agent-security/) (31/10/2025):** within one session an agent may have at most **2 of 3** properties: - [A] "process untrustworthy inputs" - [B] "access to sensitive systems or private data" - [C] "change state or communicate externally" An agent that needs all three needs human approval or must be split across sessions. Related: Simon Willison's [lethal trifecta](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/). - **GitHub Copilot coding agent, as a reference design:** - It runs in an ephemeral environment behind a firewall. - It only pushes to `copilot/*` branches. - Workflows don't run until a human approves them. - The agent cannot approve or merge its own PR. - ([GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/risks-and-mitigations)) - **OWASP:** - [LLM Top 10 2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/): LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM06 Excessive Agency. - [Agentic Top 10 2026](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/): ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation. - **Claude Code enterprise controls** (the deterministic layer, checked against code.claude.com docs): - **Delivery:** server-managed settings come from claude.ai (Organization settings → Claude Code → Managed settings), on the **Team and Enterprise** plans. They can also be delivered by MDM or through `managed-settings.json` (macOS: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/`, Linux: `/etc/claude-code/`). - **Key controls:** - `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable"` - `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowManagedHooksOnly` - `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` + `allowedMcpServers` - `strictKnownMarketplaces` - `sandbox.*` - OpenTelemetry with the endpoint locked in the managed `env` block - Section 2 has a concrete baseline. ### Summary comparison | Model | Strongest at | Weakest at | Fit for Papaya | |---|---|---|---| | 1. Google ZTP + MPA | Principles, tiering, break-glass | Very costly at full scale | Borrow the principles, not the implementation | | 2. AWS pipeline + JIT | AWS-native, cheap, mature | Doesn't cover the agent layer | ★★★★★ | | 3. Microsoft SFI/PIM/Agent ID | Agent identity, no self-escalation, planes | Azure/Entra-specific tooling | Borrow the principles, implement with IAM/SCP | | 4. GitOps + PaC | Change-management evidence, low cost | Doesn't cover debug or incidents | ★★★★★ (foundation) | | 5. Agent containment | Prompt injection, supply chain, laptop agents | Not an access model on its own | ★★★★★ (mandatory) | --- ## 2. Principal assessment: Top 3 solutions for Papaya The 5 models aren't alternatives to each other; they are building blocks. The 3 solutions below are **3 different operating architectures**, each assembled from those blocks. ### 2.1 Decision matrix Scores are 1–5; for "Effort", higher means cheaper and faster. | Criterion (weight) | S1 GitOps-gated | S2 = S1 + JIT broker | S3 Central agent runtime | |---|---|---|---| | Compliance strength (25%) | 4 | 5 | 5 | | Risk reduction (25%) | 4 | 5 | 5 | | Engineering velocity (20%) | 3 | 4 | 2 | | Effort / cost (15%) | 5 | 3 | 1 | | Fit with current stack (15%) | 5 | 4 | 2 | | **End-state score (/100)** | **82** | **87** | **67** | | Time to value | 4–6 weeks | +6 weeks after S1 | 3–6 months | **Reading the matrix:** - S2 has the highest end-state value, but it is a **superset of S1**. S1 has to exist first, and it delivers the most risk reduction per week. That is why S1 ranks #1 as the starting point and S2 is the 90-day target. - S3 is the most secure but scores worst on velocity and cost, so it is the long-term direction. ### 🥇 Solution 1 — "Agent proposes, Pipeline disposes" (GitOps-gated agents + hardened agent baseline) **Combines:** Model 4 (GitOps/PaC), Model 2 (OIDC, read-only default), Model 5 (Claude Code managed baseline), Model 3 (no self-escalation). ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Laptop["Engineer laptop · Claude Code (managed settings)"] A[Agent writes IaC / code] --> B[pulumi preview
against dev/staging] end B --> PR[PR in monorepo] PR --> CI[CI: tests, SAST, secret scan,
pulumi preview prod + CrossGuard,
sls package + CFN change-set diff] CI --> R{CODEOWNERS review
approver ≠ last pusher} R -->|approve + merge| ENV{GitHub Environment
'production'
required reviewer,
prevent self-review} ENV -->|OIDC / WIF| DEP[pulumi up · sls deploy ·
Argo CD sync · firebase deploy] DEP --> AUD[(Audit: PR + approver +
CloudTrail/GCP Audit + OTel)] Laptop -. read-only, no PHI .-> RO[(AWS/GCP/k0s prod)] Laptop -- full access --> SBX[(Sandbox/dev accounts)] ``` **How it works** 1. **Credentials on the laptop:** - Prod is reachable only through `ReadOnly-NoPHI`. It denies `s3:GetObject` on the claim-document buckets, `rds-data:*`, `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`, and `kms:Decrypt` on the PHI keys. - Remove every prod write profile from laptops. - The agent has full rights in **sandbox and dev accounts**, so Engineering keeps its speed where risk is low. 2. **The only road to prod:** - Open a PR. CI runs `pulumi preview` against prod, posts the diff on the PR, and runs CrossGuard with `mandatory` policies: public S3, wildcard IAM, disabled encryption, deleting a DB. - Don't use `remediate` on prod: auto-fixing hides the change from the reviewer. - Serverless Framework has **no built-in diff**. Run `serverless package`, create a CloudFormation change set from the template, and post it on the PR (custom step). v4 also supports `provider.deploymentMethod: changesets` ⚠️ (still need to verify whether change sets can be left unexecuted for review). - Reviews and approvals: - Ruleset "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push" + CODEOWNERS (platform and security for `infra/**`). - Environment `production` with required reviewers and Prevent self-review. - The deploy job assumes the prod role through **OIDC** with `sub = repo:papaya/:environment:production`. 3. **Multi-cloud coverage:** - **GCP (Vertex AI/Gemini):** - GitHub Actions authenticates with **Workload Identity Federation** (`google-github-actions/auth`), with an attribute condition on repository and environment. - Set org policy `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`. - Laptops get only the viewer role on prod projects. - **k0s:** - A GitOps controller (Argo CD or Flux) pulls manifests from the monorepo. - Humans and agents get a read-only kubeconfig (the `view` ClusterRole, which cannot read Secrets). - `kubectl exec`, `port-forward` and writes on prod go through JIT (S2). - **Firebase Hosting:** replace `FIREBASE_TOKEN` (the `login:ci` token) with a service account federated through WIF. 4. **Agent baseline (managed settings):** push it from the claude.ai admin console, and use MDM for the keys that must be in force before login. 5. **Shorter waits (Engineering's concern):** - A review-SLA rotation for platform reviewers. - Risk-tiered CODEOWNERS: app config is reviewed by the team, while IAM, network, data stores and KMS need platform plus security. - An agent pre-review that summarizes blast radius on the PR. It *only assists*; it is not the named approver. - Small PRs. **Illustrative baseline:** keys verified against the docs on 2026-11-05. Test against the deployed version before rollout. ```json { "forceLoginMethod": "claudeai", "forceLoginOrgUUID": "", "allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly": true, "allowManagedHooksOnly": true, "allowManagedMcpServersOnly": true, "permissions": { "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable", "deny": [ "Read(~/.ssh/**)", "Read(~/.config/gcloud/**)", "Read(./**/.env*)", "Bash(pulumi up *)", "Bash(pulumi destroy *)", "Bash(serverless deploy *)", "Bash(sls deploy *)", "Bash(firebase deploy *)", "Bash(git push --force *)", "Bash(kubectl delete *)" ] }, "allowedMcpServers": [ { "serverUrl": "https://mcp.internal.papaya.example/*" } ], "strictKnownMarketplaces": [ { "source": "github", "repo": "papaya/claude-plugins" } ], "sandbox": { "enabled": true, "failIfUnavailable": true, "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false, "network": { "allowManagedDomainsOnly": true, "allowedDomains": ["*.amazonaws.com", "*.googleapis.com", "github.com", "*.github.com", "registry.npmjs.org", "pypi.org"] }, "filesystem": { "denyRead": ["~/.ssh", "~/.config/gcloud/legacy_credentials"] } }, "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY": "1", "OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER": "otlp", "OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER": "otlp", "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL": "grpc", "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT": "https://otel.internal.papaya.example" } } ``` **Design notes:** - **Use `serverUrl`/`serverCommand`, not `serverName`.** The user picks the name, so it is not a security control. - **`strictKnownMarketplaces: []` blocks every marketplace,** including the official one. - **`forceLoginOrgUUID` must come from MDM.** Server-managed settings only arrive after login. - **`~/.aws` is deliberately not denied in the sandbox.** The agent needs the CLI to debug with the read-only role. Since laptops no longer hold any write profiles, the agent reading the RO token is acceptable (≤1h, no PHI). - **IAM is the real control; permission rules are defense-in-depth.** A deny rule can be routed around through another tool, but an IAM deny cannot. **Why it is #1** - It satisfies both quotes without trading one away. Engineers still "ship their own infra changes" through a PR, and every prod change has a named approver that GitHub records automatically. - It reuses existing tooling (monorepo, Pulumi, GitHub Actions, Claude Code). No new vendor is needed. - It closes risks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7 (via the NoPHI default) in about 4–6 weeks. **Trade-offs** | Gain | Cost | |---|---| | Strong audit trail, almost free | Every prod change waits for a reviewer, adding lead time (minutes to hours) | | Low cost, existing tooling | **Doesn't cover incidents or debugging** that need writes (restart ECS, redrive DLQ, scale) | | The agent never holds prod write credentials, which contains prompt injection | Serverless needs a custom diff step; the server-side CrossGuard features cost money | | Policy-as-code catches the agent's mistakes | Click-ops in the console sits outside GitOps. Needs drift detection plus an SCP or permission-set deny on console writes in prod | | Uniform model across AWS, GCP, k0s and Firebase | Reviewer fatigue: many agent PRs lead to rubber-stamping. Needs risk-tiering and small PRs | --- ### 🥈 Solution 2 — S1 + JIT access broker for operations (agent-aware JIT elevation) — **90-day target** **Combines:** Model 2 (JIT), Model 1 (MPA, break-glass), Model 3 (PIM-style approval, time-boxed), Model 5 (Rule of Two for debug sessions). **Adds to S1:** an operations path for work that can't go through a PR: incidents, debugging that needs data reads, and one-off runbook actions. 1. **Access tiers** (Identity Center permission sets + k0s RBAC + GCP IAM): | Tier | Purpose | TTL | Approval | |---|---|---|---| | `T0-ReadOnly-NoPHI` | Laptop default | Standing | None | | `T1-Operator` | Runbook actions: restart service, redrive DLQ, scale, invalidate cache, `kubectl rollout restart` | 1h | 1 approver; *policy-based auto-approval* if the requester is on-call and has an open incident (needs a broker that supports it) | | `T2-DataRead-PHI` | Read PHI **for a specific tenant/country** (ABAC on tags `tenant`, `country`) | 30 min | Security or DPO + ticket + justification | | `T3-BreakGlass-Admin` | Emergency | 1h | 2 approvers (MPA), alert to the security channel, mandatory postmortem, weekly review | 2. **Choosing a broker (corrected in v2):** - **AWS TEAM:** free and native. But approval is web-app only, it has no conditional auto-approval (only an on/off "Approval required" per policy), and it covers AWS only. A good fit if Compliance doesn't accept auto-approval. - **Common Fate / Granted:** CLI-first and approves in Slack. Auto-approval rules (e.g. on-call) and break-glass are written in Cedar. Covers AWS plus GCP. ⚠️ Check current pricing. - **Teleport:** if one broker should cover AWS, k0s (kubectl), DBs and SSH. Identity Governance needs Enterprise, so it is the most expensive. - **Principal call:** start with **TEAM** for AWS (zero cost, quick to prove the process). Move to Common Fate or Teleport once k0s and GCP JIT become real needs, or once Compliance accepts approval-by-policy. 3. **Making it agent-aware:** - Elevated credentials used by an agent session carry the session tags `actor=agent`, `engineer=`, `ticket=`. - An SCP or permission boundary denies `iam:*`, `organizations:*`, `sso:*`, `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion`, `rds:DeleteDBCluster` and `s3:DeleteBucket` to `actor=agent`. That rules out self-escalation and irreversible actions. - **Rule of Two for prod debug sessions:** when the agent reads logs or data on prod, it has [A] untrusted input (logs contain text from partner documents) and possibly [B] sensitive data. It must therefore **not have [C]**: no write role, and egress limited to the AWS endpoints and the model endpoint. To act on what it finds, open a new session with T1, or go back to a PR. 4. **HIPAA gate (corrected in v2), required before opening T2 to agents:** - Anthropic's BAA covers Claude Code only on the **Enterprise plan with HIPAA activated**: the Primary Owner accepts the BAA, applies the HIPAA configuration, and members sign in with Enterprise accounts. The **Team plan is not addressed**. - Claude Code through **Bedrock/Vertex/a gateway is not covered by Anthropic's BAA**. Bedrock is on AWS's HIPAA-eligible services list, so coverage would come from **Papaya's AWS BAA** ⚠️ (confirm per model in AWS Artifact). - **Options:** - (a) Upgrade to Enterprise + HIPAA config. - (b) Route PHI-touching sessions through Claude on Bedrock under the AWS BAA. - (c) **Agents never get T2.** Only humans read PHI. Until Legal decides, **(c) is the default**. **Why #2 (and the target end state)** - It answers Engineering's real need, "I want to debug… without waiting", which S1 doesn't cover. - It keeps Compliance's principle: every elevation has a named approver, or an approval-by-policy that a named person signed off in advance, plus expiry and logs. - It makes on-call formal (risk 5), because elevation is tied to incidents. - T3 break-glass directly meets HIPAA 164.312(a)(2)(ii) *Emergency access procedure*, a **Required** implementation specification. **Trade-offs** | Gain | Cost | |---|---| | Covers incidents and debugging, so engineers have no reason to want "standing prod admin" | More moving parts (broker, tier policies, SCPs, Slack): +6 weeks of effort | | Time-boxed, so a leaked credential has little value | Policy design is easy to get wrong: T1 too broad becomes standing admin; T1 too narrow sends everyone to T3 | | Agent sessions are tagged, so CloudTrail separates agents from humans | TEAM has no approve-in-Slack and no conditional auto-approval, so the incident experience is slower; upgrading the broker costs money | | Rule of Two contains prompt injection during debugging | T1 changes are *not in git*. Drift has to be reconciled: the next PR codifies the change or it gets reverted | | ABAC per tenant/country fits multi-partner contracts | Approval-by-policy needs written acceptance from Compliance | --- ### 🥉 Solution 3 — Centralized Agent Runtime: agents run on managed infrastructure, laptops hold no cloud credentials **Combines:** Model 5 (Copilot-coding-agent-style sandbox), Model 1 (agent = workload identity, BeyondProd), Model 3 (dedicated agent identity), Model 2 (Scoping Matrix scope 2→3). **How it works** - **Runners:** every infra-capable agent task (IaC changes, prod debugging, runbooks) runs on **ephemeral runners**: GitHub Actions with the Claude Code Action, or devcontainers on EC2/k0s pods. - **Identity:** each task type and environment gets its own **agent identity**, an IAM role or GCP service account obtained through OIDC/WIF. - **Triggers:** Linear, Slack, or a PR comment. - **Laptops** hold **no cloud credentials at all**. Claude Code on the laptop only writes code, runs tests and pushes branches. - **Hardening:** - Firewalled egress with an allowlist. - Credentials scoped to the task with a 15–60 minute TTL. - Full transcripts stored in S3 with Object Lock. - MCP servers come only from a container image curated by the platform team. - **Approval gate:** - The agent posts a plan. - A named approver approves it through a GitHub Environment. - Only then does the job receive write credentials. - **CI-specific risk (prompt injection in CI):** PR content, issues and comments are all [A] untrusted input. - Never use `pull_request_target` combined with checking out the PR head. - Only members with write access can trigger the agent. - An agent job that reads untrusted content gets a read-only token and no prod credentials. Its output is just a PR, which goes back through S1's gates. **Why #3** - **Strongest security:** laptops are removed from the trust boundary, the attack surface is fixed, and evidence is centralized. It also matches where the industry is going (Copilot coding agent, Claude Code GitHub Action, background agents). - **Too early for Papaya:** - The effort is high: runner platform, image pipeline, secret brokering, transcript storage. - It breaks the local dev loop. - Without the S1/S2 baseline in place, Engineering is likely to bypass it and fall into the "shadow agent" anti-pattern. **Trade-offs** | Gain | Cost | |---|---| | No credentials on laptops; a lost laptop never touches the cloud | Highest effort (3–6 months) plus a team to operate the runner platform | | Uniform, reproducible environment with centrally managed MCP | Interactive debugging is slower than local (latency, context) | | Complete, immutable audit transcripts, strong for HIPAA/ISO | Compute plus background tokens cost more | | Easy to apply Rule of Two per job type | Runners hold prod roles, which makes them high-value targets; they need isolation and pinned images | | | The CI attack surface gets bigger (prompt injection through PRs and issues) | **Principal view:** S3 is the **18-month direction** for *autonomous/background* tasks (dependency upgrades, drift remediation, PRs generated from alerts). It does not replace S1+S2. --- ## 3. Tôi đã sửa xong báo cáo (bản v2) và đẩy lên GitHub: [minhhieu16/DevSecOps_Challenge](https://github.com/minhhieu16/DevSecOps_Challenge), nhánh `main`, gồm 1 commit.

**Những gì thay đổi trong báo cáo**

Tôi dùng 3 sub-agent để kiểm tra lại các mục ⚠️ với nguồn gốc. Các điểm sửa quan trọng:

- **HIPAA, đây là thay đổi lớn nhất:**
  - BAA của Anthropic chỉ bao Claude Code trên gói **Enterprise** khi đã bật cấu hình HIPAA. Gói Team, gói Papaya đang dùng, không được nhắc tới.
  - Claude Code chạy qua Bedrock hay Vertex **không** nằm trong BAA của Anthropic. Nếu đi qua Bedrock thì phải dựa vào BAA của AWS.
  - Vì vậy báo cáo thêm một cửa pháp lý ở Phase 0. Trong lúc chờ Legal quyết, mặc định là agent không bao giờ được đọc PHI.
- **AWS TEAM:** việc duyệt chỉ làm trên web app, Slack chỉ dùng để gửi thông báo. TEAM cũng không tự duyệt theo điều kiện (ví dụ "đang on-call và có incident"). Tôi đã sửa phần chọn broker ở Giải pháp 2: bắt đầu bằng TEAM, khi cần thì nâng lên Common Fate hoặc Teleport.
- **Bổ sung các phần còn thiếu:**
  - **Đa cloud:** GCP và Firebase dùng Workload Identity Federation thay cho key; k0s dùng Argo CD/Flux với kubeconfig chỉ đọc.
  - **Ma trận chấm điểm có trọng số:** S1 = 82, S2 = 87, S3 = 67.
  - **Bảng đối chiếu tuân thủ** với các control ISO 27001:2022 Annex A và HIPAA 164.312. Break-glass ở S2 đáp ứng trực tiếp *Emergency access procedure* (Required).

input.new_string:
- **IAM is the real control; permission rules are defense-in-depth.** A deny rule can be routed around through another tool, but an IAM deny cannot.

#### Config & secret changes (added in v2.1)

Parameters, feature flags and secrets **are prod changes** under Compliance's rule. They are also the easiest path around GitOps: one `aws ssm put-parameter` or one edit in the Secrets Manager console changes prod behavior with no PR. The design rests on two principles:

> **P1. Every config/secret *definition* lives in git and goes through the same PR flow. Secret *values* never live in git.**
> **P2. Secret values never pass through the agent's context.** The agent can create or change a secret's *definition* through a PR, but never reads or writes the *value*. Anything that enters the context is sent to the model provider and may end up in a transcript or log.

**Classification and handling:**

| Change type | Examples | Source of truth | Who changes it, and how | Approval | Agent allowed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Non-secret config** | Timeouts, batch sizes, endpoints, per-tenant/country config | Git: `Pulumi.<stack>.yaml`, `serverless.yml` params, k0s ConfigMap via Argo CD | PR → pipeline | Same as code: CODEOWNERS + Environment `production` | ✅ Writes the PR |
| **Feature flags / runtime config** | Enable a model for a partner, FWA thresholds | Git → **AWS AppConfig** (validators + deployment strategy + rollback on CloudWatch alarm) | PR → pipeline triggers an AppConfig deployment | PR approver; changes to claim/FWA thresholds also need product/risk in CODEOWNERS | ✅ Writes the PR |
| **Secret definition** | Name and path `/papaya/{env}/{tenant}/...`, KMS key, resource policy, which roles can read it, rotation schedule | Git (Pulumi: `aws.secretsmanager.Secret`, `SecretRotation`; GCP `secretmanager.Secret`) | PR → pipeline | CODEOWNERS = platform + security | ✅ Writes the PR (no value) |
| **Secret value: machine-generated** | Aurora password, internal service tokens | Generated by AWS: RDS **managed master user password** in Secrets Manager, rotation Lambda | Automatic rotation; nobody ever sees the value | The rotation policy is approved through a PR (definition); each rotation is logged | ❌ |
| **Secret value: from a third party** | Partner API keys, OpenAI/Gemini keys, bank/payment credentials | Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager | A human (the integration owner) through **JIT tier `T1-SecretWriter`**, or the **"secret-intake" workflow** (below) | Approver ≠ writer + Linear ticket | ❌ |
| **Emergency rotation (leak)** | A token leaked in a log or a commit | — | `workflow_dispatch` "rotate-secret" → Environment approval → the job calls `RotateSecret` / re-issues the key; nobody sees the new value | 1 approver (runbook); post-incident review | ❌ Agent may only *open the incident* |

**Mechanics:**

1. **Runtime injection, not deploy-time.** Applications read secrets at runtime:
   - Lambda: the Parameters & Secrets extension or the SDK.
   - ECS: the `secrets` field (`valueFrom` ARN) in the task definition.
   - k0s: **External Secrets Operator** syncs from AWS SM / GCP SM, so no `Secret` manifests live in git.
   - **Serverless gotcha:** `${ssm:/path}` (including SecureString) is resolved **at deploy time** and written as **plaintext** into the CloudFormation template and the Lambda env vars. That makes it visible in the PR diff, the console, and to the read-only role. Pass the ARN or parameter name and fetch at runtime ⚠️ (confirm the exact behavior on Serverless v4).
2. **Policy-as-code blocks leaking values into templates:**
   - CrossGuard `mandatory` rules:
     - Lambda/ECS env vars whose keys match `*SECRET*|*TOKEN*|*PASSWORD*|*KEY*` are rejected unless they are ARNs.
     - Every `Secret` must have a KMS CMK, a resource policy, and rotation (unless it carries the tag `rotation=manual-thirdparty`).
     - Every `Secret` must carry the tags `owner`, `tenant`, and `data-class`.
   - Pulumi state contains secret values (encrypted by the secrets provider), so the state backend is a sensitive asset. Use a KMS secrets provider, and limit state access to the pipeline role.
3. **The secret-intake workflow:** for third-party values with no human or agent in the middle:
   - The integration owner opens a Linear ticket.
   - The pipeline creates the secret definition (PR) and sets a placeholder value.
   - The owner pastes the value directly in the Secrets Manager console with the `T1-SecretWriter` role (JIT, 15 minutes, scoped to *that* secret ARN through ABAC tags) after approval.
   - The partner can also push through a one-time pre-signed upload, if that is in the contract.
4. **Detection (the detective control that completes P1):** EventBridge + CloudTrail raise an alert in the SIEM/Slack when any of these come from a principal that is **not** the pipeline role, the rotation role, or an approved session of `T1-SecretWriter`:
   - `PutSecretValue`, `UpdateSecret`, `DeleteSecret`, `PutParameter`, `DeleteParameter`
   - `UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (env change)
   - GCP `AddSecretVersion`

   Every alert must map to a ticket, or it becomes an incident.
5. **GitHub Actions secrets:** after the OIDC/WIF migration, any tokens left over (third parties with no OIDC) go into **environment secrets** for `production`, so only jobs that passed the environment approval can read them. Turn on **secret scanning + push protection** for the monorepo, and run gitleaks in CI.
6. **Agents and secrets in practice:**
   - The deny rules in the baseline block the agent from reading or writing values.
   - When the agent needs a new secret, it writes the PR for the definition plus the application code that reads it at runtime, then *tells the engineer* to put the value in through the intake workflow.
   - If an engineer pastes a secret into a prompt, treat it as **leaked** and rotate it (written into the onboarding playbook).

**Why it is #1**

toolUseResult.newString:
- **IAM is the real control; permission rules are defense-in-depth.** A deny rule can be routed around through another tool, but an IAM deny cannot.

#### Config & secret changes (added in v2.1)

Parameters, feature flags and secrets **are prod changes** under Compliance's rule. They are also the easiest path around GitOps: one `aws ssm put-parameter` or one edit in the Secrets Manager console changes prod behavior with no PR. The design rests on two principles:

> **P1. Every config/secret *definition* lives in git and goes through the same PR flow. Secret *values* never live in git.**
> **P2. Secret values never pass through the agent's context.** The agent can create or change a secret's *definition* through a PR, but never reads or writes the *value*. Anything that enters the context is sent to the model provider and may end up in a transcript or log.

**Classification and handling:**

| Change type | Examples | Source of truth | Who changes it, and how | Approval | Agent allowed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Non-secret config** | Timeouts, batch sizes, endpoints, per-tenant/country config | Git: `Pulumi.<stack>.yaml`, `serverless.yml` params, k0s ConfigMap via Argo CD | PR → pipeline | Same as code: CODEOWNERS + Environment `production` | ✅ Writes the PR |
| **Feature flags / runtime config** | Enable a model for a partner, FWA thresholds | Git → **AWS AppConfig** (validators + deployment strategy + rollback on CloudWatch alarm) | PR → pipeline triggers an AppConfig deployment | PR approver; changes to claim/FWA thresholds also need product/risk in CODEOWNERS | ✅ Writes the PR |
| **Secret definition** | Name and path `/papaya/{env}/{tenant}/...`, KMS key, resource policy, which roles can read it, rotation schedule | Git (Pulumi: `aws.secretsmanager.Secret`, `SecretRotation`; GCP `secretmanager.Secret`) | PR → pipeline | CODEOWNERS = platform + security | ✅ Writes the PR (no value) |
| **Secret value: machine-generated** | Aurora password, internal service tokens | Generated by AWS: RDS **managed master user password** in Secrets Manager, rotation Lambda | Automatic rotation; nobody ever sees the value | The rotation policy is approved through a PR (definition); each rotation is logged | ❌ |
| **Secret value: from a third party** | Partner API keys, OpenAI/Gemini keys, bank/payment credentials | Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager | A human (the integration owner) through **JIT tier `T1-SecretWriter`**, or the **"secret-intake" workflow** (below) | Approver ≠ writer + Linear ticket | ❌ |
| **Emergency rotation (leak)** | A token leaked in a log or a commit | — | `workflow_dispatch` "rotate-secret" → Environment approval → the job calls `RotateSecret` / re-issues the key; nobody sees the new value | 1 approver (runbook); post-incident review | ❌ Agent may only *open the incident* |

**Mechanics:**

1. **Runtime injection, not deploy-time.** Applications read secrets at runtime:
   - Lambda: the Parameters & Secrets extension or the SDK.
   - ECS: the `secrets` field (`valueFrom` ARN) in the task definition.
   - k0s: **External Secrets Operator** syncs from AWS SM / GCP SM, so no `Secret` manifests live in git.
   - **Serverless gotcha:** `${ssm:/path}` (including SecureString) is resolved **at deploy time** and written as **plaintext** into the CloudFormation template and the Lambda env vars. That makes it visible in the PR diff, the console, and to the read-only role. Pass the ARN or parameter name and fetch at runtime ⚠️ (confirm the exact behavior on Serverless v4).
2. **Policy-as-code blocks leaking values into templates:**
   - CrossGuard `mandatory` rules:
     - Lambda/ECS env vars whose keys match `*SECRET*|*TOKEN*|*PASSWORD*|*KEY*` are rejected unless they are ARNs.
     - Every `Secret` must have a KMS CMK, a resource policy, and rotation (unless it carries the tag `rotation=manual-thirdparty`).
     - Every `Secret` must carry the tags `owner`, `tenant`, and `data-class`.
   - Pulumi state contains secret values (encrypted by the secrets provider), so the state backend is a sensitive asset. Use a KMS secrets provider, and limit state access to the pipeline role.
3. **The secret-intake workflow:** for third-party values with no human or agent in the middle:
   - The integration owner opens a Linear ticket.
   - The pipeline creates the secret definition (PR) and sets a placeholder value.
   - The owner pastes the value directly in the Secrets Manager console with the `T1-SecretWriter` role (JIT, 15 minutes, scoped to *that* secret ARN through ABAC tags) after approval.
   - The partner can also push through a one-time pre-signed upload, if that is in the contract.
4. **Detection (the detective control that completes P1):** EventBridge + CloudTrail raise an alert in the SIEM/Slack when any of these come from a principal that is **not** the pipeline role, the rotation role, or an approved session of `T1-SecretWriter`:
   - `PutSecretValue`, `UpdateSecret`, `DeleteSecret`, `PutParameter`, `DeleteParameter`
   - `UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (env change)
   - GCP `AddSecretVersion`

   Every alert must map to a ticket, or it becomes an incident.
5. **GitHub Actions secrets:** after the OIDC/WIF migration, any tokens left over (third parties with no OIDC) go into **environment secrets** for `production`, so only jobs that passed the environment approval can read them. Turn on **secret scanning + push protection** for the monorepo, and run gitleaks in CI.
6. **Agents and secrets in practice:**
   - The deny rules in the baseline block the agent from reading or writing values.
   - When the agent needs a new secret, it writes the PR for the definition plus the application code that reads it at runtime, then *tells the engineer* to put the value in through the intake workflow.
   - If an engineer pastes a secret into a prompt, treat it as **leaked** and rotate it (written into the onboarding playbook).

**Why it is #1**

input.new_string:
- **IAM is the real control; permission rules are defense-in-depth.** A deny rule can be routed around through another tool, but an IAM deny cannot.

#### Config & secret changes (added in v2.1)

Parameters, feature flags and secrets **are prod changes** under Compliance's rule. They are also the easiest path around GitOps: one `aws ssm put-parameter` or one edit in the Secrets Manager console changes prod behavior with no PR. The design rests on two principles:

> **P1. Every config/secret *definition* lives in git and goes through the same PR flow. Secret *values* never live in git.**
> **P2. Secret values never pass through the agent's context.** The agent can create or change a secret's *definition* through a PR, but never reads or writes the *value*. Anything that enters the context is sent to the model provider and may end up in a transcript or log.

**Classification and handling:**

| Change type | Examples | Source of truth | Who changes it, and how | Approval | Agent allowed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Non-secret config** | Timeouts, batch sizes, endpoints, per-tenant/country config | Git: `Pulumi.<stack>.yaml`, `serverless.yml` params, k0s ConfigMap via Argo CD | PR → pipeline | Same as code: CODEOWNERS + Environment `production` | ✅ Writes the PR |
| **Feature flags / runtime config** | Enable a model for a partner, FWA thresholds | Git → **AWS AppConfig** (validators + deployment strategy + rollback on CloudWatch alarm) | PR → pipeline triggers an AppConfig deployment | PR approver; changes to claim/FWA thresholds also need product/risk in CODEOWNERS | ✅ Writes the PR |
| **Secret definition** | Name and path `/papaya/{env}/{tenant}/...`, KMS key, resource policy, which roles can read it, rotation schedule | Git (Pulumi: `aws.secretsmanager.Secret`, `SecretRotation`; GCP `secretmanager.Secret`) | PR → pipeline | CODEOWNERS = platform + security | ✅ Writes the PR (no value) |
| **Secret value: machine-generated** | Aurora password, internal service tokens | Generated by AWS: RDS **managed master user password** in Secrets Manager, rotation Lambda | Automatic rotation; nobody ever sees the value | The rotation policy is approved through a PR (definition); each rotation is logged | ❌ |
| **Secret value: from a third party** | Partner API keys, OpenAI/Gemini keys, bank/payment credentials | Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager | A human (the integration owner) through **JIT tier `T1-SecretWriter`**, or the **"secret-intake" workflow** (below) | Approver ≠ writer + Linear ticket | ❌ |
| **Emergency rotation (leak)** | A token leaked in a log or a commit | — | `workflow_dispatch` "rotate-secret" → Environment approval → the job calls `RotateSecret` / re-issues the key; nobody sees the new value | 1 approver (runbook); post-incident review | ❌ Agent may only *open the incident* |

**Mechanics:**

1. **Runtime injection, not deploy-time.** Applications read secrets at runtime:
   - Lambda: the Parameters & Secrets extension or the SDK.
   - ECS: the `secrets` field (`valueFrom` ARN) in the task definition.
   - k0s: **External Secrets Operator** syncs from AWS SM / GCP SM, so no `Secret` manifests live in git.
   - **Serverless gotcha:** `${ssm:/path}` (including SecureString) is resolved **at deploy time** and written as **plaintext** into the CloudFormation template and the Lambda env vars. That makes it visible in the PR diff, the console, and to the read-only role. Pass the ARN or parameter name and fetch at runtime ⚠️ (confirm the exact behavior on Serverless v4).
2. **Policy-as-code blocks leaking values into templates:**
   - CrossGuard `mandatory` rules:
     - Lambda/ECS env vars whose keys match `*SECRET*|*TOKEN*|*PASSWORD*|*KEY*` are rejected unless they are ARNs.
     - Every `Secret` must have a KMS CMK, a resource policy, and rotation (unless it carries the tag `rotation=manual-thirdparty`).
     - Every `Secret` must carry the tags `owner`, `tenant`, and `data-class`.
   - Pulumi state contains secret values (encrypted by the secrets provider), so the state backend is a sensitive asset. Use a KMS secrets provider, and limit state access to the pipeline role.
3. **The secret-intake workflow:** for third-party values with no human or agent in the middle:
   - The integration owner opens a Linear ticket.
   - The pipeline creates the secret definition (PR) and sets a placeholder value.
   - The owner pastes the value directly in the Secrets Manager console with the `T1-SecretWriter` role (JIT, 15 minutes, scoped to *that* secret ARN through ABAC tags) after approval.
   - The partner can also push through a one-time pre-signed upload, if that is in the contract.
4. **Detection (the detective control that completes P1):** EventBridge + CloudTrail raise an alert in the SIEM/Slack when any of these come from a principal that is **not** the pipeline role, the rotation role, or an approved session of `T1-SecretWriter`:
   - `PutSecretValue`, `UpdateSecret`, `DeleteSecret`, `PutParameter`, `DeleteParameter`
   - `UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (env change)
   - GCP `AddSecretVersion`

   Every alert must map to a ticket, or it becomes an incident.
5. **GitHub Actions secrets:** after the OIDC/WIF migration, any tokens left over (third parties with no OIDC) go into **environment secrets** for `production`, so only jobs that passed the environment approval can read them. Turn on **secret scanning + push protection** for the monorepo, and run gitleaks in CI.
6. **Agents and secrets in practice:**
   - The deny rules in the baseline block the agent from reading or writing values.
   - When the agent needs a new secret, it writes the PR for the definition plus the application code that reads it at runtime, then *tells the engineer* to put the value in through the intake workflow.
   - If an engineer pastes a secret into a prompt, treat it as **leaked** and rotate it (written into the onboarding playbook).

**Why it is #1**

Bạn nói đúng, bản v2 bỏ sót mảng này. Tôi đã thêm mục **"Config & secret changes"** vào Giải pháp 1 và nâng báo cáo lên v2.1. Thay đổi mới nằm ở máy local, chưa commit hay push.

Parameter, feature flag và secret đều là thay đổi prod. Chúng cũng là đường dễ nhất để lách GitOps, vì một lệnh `aws ssm put-parameter` là đổi được prod mà không cần PR. Thiết kế dựa trên 2 nguyên tắc:

- **P1. Định nghĩa nằm trong git, giá trị nằm trong vault.** Tên secret, KMS key, role nào được đọc và lịch rotation đều đi qua PR như code. Giá trị secret không bao giờ nằm trong git.
- **P2. Giá trị secret không bao giờ đi qua context của agent.** Agent được viết PR cho phần định nghĩa nhưng không đọc hay ghi giá trị. Mọi thứ vào context đều được gửi tới nhà cung cấp model.

**Xử lý theo từng loại thay đổi:**

| Loại | Nguồn sự thật | Cách thay đổi | Agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config thường | Git (Pulumi stack config, `serverless.yml`, ConfigMap) | PR rồi pipeline | ✅ |
| Feature flag, ngưỡng FWA | Git, deploy qua AWS AppConfig (có validator và rollback khi alarm) | PR; ngưỡng FWA cần thêm reviewer bên product/risk | ✅ |
| Định nghĩa secret | Git (Pulumi) | PR, platform và security duyệt | ✅ (không có giá trị) |
| Secret do máy sinh (mật khẩu Aurora, token nội bộ) | AWS tự sinh và rotate | Không ai nhìn thấy giá trị | ❌ |
| Secret của bên thứ ba (API của partner, OpenAI) | Secrets Manager | Người phụ trách nhập qua JIT `T1-SecretWriter` (15 phút, chỉ cho đúng một secret, người duyệt khác người nhập) | ❌ |
| Rotate khẩn cấp khi lộ | — | Workflow "rotate-secret" có bước duyệt; không ai thấy giá trị mới | ❌ |

**Hai lỗ hổng đáng chú ý khi rà phần này:**

1. **Role read-only ở bản v2 vẫn đọc được secret.** Policy `ReadOnlyAccess` do AWS quản lý cho đọc biến môi trường của Lambda, env trong task definition của ECS và SSM parameter. Nếu secret nằm trong env var thì "read-only" cũng đồng nghĩa với đọc được secret. Tôi đã sửa sang policy read-only tự viết, và chặn thêm việc đọc SecureString trong SSM.
2. **Biến `${ssm:/path}` của Serverless được resolve lúc deploy** và ghi plaintext vào CloudFormation template và env của Lambda. Hệ quả là secret hiện trong diff của PR. Cách sửa là chuyển sang đọc secret lúc runtime.

**Các phần khác đã cập nhật:**
- Policy-as-code (CrossGuard) chặn env var có tên giống secret.
- External Secrets Operator cho k0s.
- Cảnh báo CloudTrail khi có `PutSecretValue` hoặc `PutParameter` không đi qua pipeline.
- Bật secret scanning và push protection.
- Bổ sung luật deny trong managed settings, tier `T1-SecretWriter` ở Giải pháp 2, control ISO A.5.17 và A.8.24, Phase 1 của roadmap và một câu hỏi mở mới.

Hai điểm (về `ReadOnlyAccess` và hành vi của `${ssm:}`) dựa trên hiểu biết của tôi, chưa kiểm với tài liệu gốc. Tôi đã đánh ⚠️ trong Appendix B.

1. AWS IAM: not all actions support resource-level permissions; for such actions the resource is "*", so a Deny statement with a specific Resource ARN pattern (e.g. arn:aws:lambda:*:*:function:prod-*) does not apply to them. Examples: lambda:ListFunctions, ec2:DescribeInstances. Cite the Service Authorization Reference.

3. AWS STS session tags: `aws sts assume-role --tags` requires sts:TagSession in the trust policy; tags appear in CloudTrail; transitive tags.
4. AWS-managed policy ReadOnlyAccess includes lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration (exposes env vars), ecs:DescribeTaskDefinition, ssm:GetParameter(s). Check the managed policy reference page.

6. GCP IAM Deny policies: exist (IAM v2), attach to org/folder/project, support exception principals and denial conditions on resource tags.

input.content:
# Papaya — Coding Agents for DevSecOps: Big-Tech Models & Top 3 Solutions

> Role: Principal DevSecOps · Version: **v3** · Date: 2026-11-05
> Method: 5 research sub-agents (3× Sonnet, 2× Haiku) → orchestrator synthesis → fact-check sub-agents against primary sources → revisions with the candidate's input.
> Verification status of every non-obvious claim is in [Appendix B](#appendix-b--verification-status). Remaining ⚠️ items are flagged inline.

### Changelog

- **v3:** the operating model is **simplified to 2 environments (nonprod / prod)**, with the naming convention `<env>-<service>-<name>` (SSM: `/<env>/<service>/<name>`) and **IAM deny on `prod-*`**. Troubleshooting and debugging are an **exception governed by detective controls**: telemetry flows into a **central SIEM built on Google SecOps**. §2 is a principal review of this proposal (strengths, gaps, refinements). S1 and S2 are rewritten around the model, and §4 adds the SecOps telemetry and detection architecture.
- **v2.1:** config and secret changes: "definition in git, value in vault", and secret values never pass through the agent's context.
- **v2:** HIPAA/BAA scope corrected, AWS TEAM corrected, multi-cloud (GCP, k0s, Firebase), decision matrix, compliance mapping, verified Claude Code baseline.

---

## 0. Diagnosis: Papaya's actual problem

| # | Current state | Risk | Applicable framework |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Laptop SSO profile reaches prod, and the agent inherits it | Agent = an engineer with prod rights; a prompt injection or bad command hits prod directly | Google Zero-Touch Prod; AWS "read-only default + JIT" |
| 2 | Permission prompts turned off | No deterministic control between the model and the shell | OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency; Claude Code managed settings |
| 3 | MCP servers and plugins unreviewed | Supply chain, tool poisoning, credential theft | OWASP LLM03 / ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain |
| 4 | Long-lived GitHub token and AWS keys in CI secrets | One leak gives persistent, unattributed access | Microsoft SFI; OIDC / Workload Identity Federation |
| 5 | Monitoring fragmented (CloudWatch, GCP, Slack); on-call informal | No evidence for ISO A.8.15/A.8.16 or HIPAA 164.312(b); slow detection | Central SIEM (Google SecOps); Google "observable actions" |
| 6 | Production AI agents read partner/member documents | Untrusted input + PHI + ability to change claim state invites prompt injection | Meta "Agents Rule of Two"; lethal trifecta |
| 7 | Coding agents may read PHI and send it to the model provider | HIPAA exposure if the plan or channel isn't covered by a BAA | Anthropic BAA scope; AWS BAA for Bedrock |

**Key point:** the Engineering vs Compliance conflict is not a dilemma. Every big-tech model resolves it the same way:

> **Agents and humans get broad freedom to *propose* and *observe*; only an attributable pipeline or broker *executes* changes on prod, after a named person approves.**

Compliance's wording is about **changes** ("Nothing *changes* in production…"). That distinction is what makes the v3 model work. **Observing prod** (debugging) can be governed by detective controls. **Changing prod** needs preventive controls plus a named approver.

---

## 1. Top 5 models used at large organizations

### Model 1 — Google: Zero-Touch Prod + Multi-Party Authorization (BeyondProd / BAB)

- **Core idea:** no human holds standing access to prod. Every change goes through automation or small, safe APIs, and sensitive actions need a second person's approval (MPA). Code reaches prod only if it was reviewed and built on an isolated system with provenance (Binary Authorization for Borg).
- **Key controls:**
  - Risk tiering.
  - MPA on *specific actions*.
  - A proxy for commands that lack fine-grained APIs.
  - Break-glass that is monitored, tested regularly, and peer-reviewed every week.
  - Logs with a justification (ticket ID).
- **Agents:** every agent has a *human controller*, *limited powers*, and *observable* actions.
- **Transferable:** default-deny for prod writes, narrow tools instead of a raw shell, and linking each agent run to its approver and its change. **Not worth it:** full ZTP, a self-built BAB, or a service mesh everywhere.
- **Sources:** [BSRS ch.5](https://google.github.io/building-secure-and-reliable-systems/raw/ch05.html) · [BAB](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/binary-authorization-for-borg) · [Google secure AI agents](https://research.google/pubs/an-introduction-to-googles-approach-for-secure-ai-agents/) · [SAIF agent self-assessment](https://saif.google/agent-risk-self-assessment)

### Model 2 — Amazon/AWS: "Humans don't deploy, pipelines do" + read-only default + JIT

- **Core idea:** code review is the last manual gate. Pipelines deploy in waves, with bake time and automatic rollback on alarm. People get **read-only by default**, and writes go through JIT: request, approval, expiry.
- **Key controls:**
  - [TEAM](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-identity-center-team):
    - Approvers are Identity Center groups, and self-approval is blocked.
    - Duration is set per policy, and each eligibility policy has an "Approval required" toggle.
    - **Approval happens in the web app.** Slack is notification-only.
  - SCPs and permission boundaries.
  - GitHub OIDC with a strict `sub` (`repo:ORG/REPO:environment:production`).
- **Agents:** the [Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix](https://aws.amazon.com/ai/security/agentic-ai-scoping-matrix/) puts a coding agent at **Scope 2: Prescribed Agency**, with enforcement outside the model.
  - `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` (Bool) and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` (String) only apply to calls through an AWS-managed MCP service.
  - A CLI call made by Claude Code on a laptop looks like a human call. Separate roles plus SourceIdentity are the real control (§3).
- **Sources:** [Hands-off deployments](https://builder.aws.com/content/3ErTKQOTKc5NIw031UePBPxTQ6I/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments) · [AG.SAD.4](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/devops-guidance/ag.sad.4-limit-human-access-with-just-in-time-access.html) · [TEAM docs](https://aws-samples.github.io/iam-identity-center-team/docs/overview/workflow.html) · [IAM condition keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html)

### Model 3 — Microsoft: SFI + PIM/JIT + Enterprise Access Model + dedicated agent identities

- **Core idea:** secure by design, by default, and in operations. Remove long-lived secrets and isolate credentials.
- **PIM:** approvers cannot approve their own requests, service principals cannot approve, and activation is time-bound. The control, management and data planes are separated.
- **Entra Agent ID:** agents are their own identity type and can never hold high-privilege roles.
- **Transferable:** "**an agent can never grant itself privileges**". Deny `iam:*`, `organizations:*` and `sso:*` to agent sessions.
- **Sources:** [SFI 07/2026](https://microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/10/securing-our-future-july-2026-progress-report-on-microsofts-secure-future-initiative) · [PIM approval](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-approval-workflow) · [Entra Agent ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/authorization-agent-id)

### Model 4 — GitOps + Policy-as-Code: "the PR is the only road to prod"

- **Core idea:** plan on the PR, run the policy check, get human review, and apply after merge. The approval is the PR review by a named person.
- **Tooling:**
  - Pulumi CrossGuard: `advisory`, `mandatory`, `remediate`, `disabled`. Local `--policy-pack` is free, while server-side enforcement is paid.
  - GitHub rulesets: "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push" + CODEOWNERS.
  - Environments: required reviewers + **Prevent self-review**.
- **Weakness:** it only covers changes that go through git.
- **Sources:** [CrossGuard](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/crossguard/configuration/) · [GitHub rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets) · [Environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/managing-workflow-runs-and-deployments/managing-deployments/managing-environments-for-deployment)

### Model 5 — Agent containment: Meta "Rule of Two" + Copilot coding-agent sandbox + OWASP + Claude Code managed settings

- **[Meta Agents Rule of Two](https://ai.meta.com/blog/practical-ai-agent-security/) (31/10/2025):** in one session an agent has at most 2 of these 3:
  - [A] processes untrusted input
  - [B] accesses sensitive data or systems
  - [C] changes state or communicates externally
- **GitHub Copilot coding agent:**
  - Runs in an ephemeral environment with a firewall.
  - Pushes only to `copilot/*`.
  - Workflows wait for a human to approve.
  - Cannot approve its own PR.
- **OWASP:** [LLM Top 10 2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/) (LLM01, LLM02, LLM03, LLM06). [Agentic Top 10 2026](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) (ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation).
- **Claude Code:**
  - Server-managed settings (Team and Enterprise) + MDM.
  - `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable"`, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, `allowManagedMcpServersOnly`, `strictKnownMarketplaces`, `sandbox.*`.
  - OTel with the endpoint locked.

### Summary comparison

| Model | Strongest at | Weakest at | Fit for Papaya |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Google ZTP + MPA | Principles, break-glass | Very costly at full scale | Borrow the principles |
| 2. AWS pipeline + JIT | AWS-native, cheap | Doesn't cover the agent layer | ★★★★★ |
| 3. Microsoft SFI/PIM/Agent ID | No self-escalation | Entra-specific tooling | Borrow the principles |
| 4. GitOps + PaC | Change-management evidence | Doesn't cover debug | ★★★★★ (foundation) |
| 5. Agent containment | Prompt injection, supply chain | Not an access model | ★★★★★ (mandatory) |

---

## 2. Principal review of the proposed operating model

### 2.1 The proposal

1. **Two environments only: `nonprod` and `prod`.**
2. **Naming convention:** resources are `<env>-<service>-<name>` (e.g. `prod-claim-ingest`), SSM is `/<env>/<service>/<name>`.
3. **Preventive rule:** IAM **denies every action on `prod-*`** for humans and agents.
4. **Exception:** troubleshooting and debugging on prod are allowed, but **every action is instrumented** (telemetry and metrics) and sent to central storage.
5. **Architecture:** the central store is a SIEM modeled on **Google SecOps**.

### 2.2 What is strong (keep)

- **Simple enough to explain, audit and enforce.** Two environments mean two rule sets, and an auditor or new engineer understands it in five minutes. It maps directly to ISO A.8.31 *Separation of development, test and production environments*.
- **Default deny on prod** is the core of Models 1 and 2. A prompt injection on a laptop no longer has a path to change prod.
- **Separating observing from changing** fits the wording of Compliance's statement exactly. Debugging doesn't need preventive approval, so Engineering isn't blocked on troubleshooting. That is the real pain behind "without waiting for someone else".
- **A central SIEM** solves risk 5 (fragmented monitoring) and produces the audit evidence that HIPAA 164.312(b) and ISO A.8.15/A.8.16 require. Google SecOps fits because Papaya already runs on GCP and it ingests AWS, GCP, GitHub and Kubernetes sources.
- **The naming convention** also helps telemetry: SIEM rules and dashboards can classify an event as prod or nonprod straight from the resource name or SSM path.

### 2.3 Gaps and how to close them

| # | Gap | Why it matters | Refinement |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G1** | **Name matching is not a complete IAM boundary.** Many actions don't support resource-level permissions: the resource is `*` for `List*` and many `Describe*` actions. A deny on `arn:…:prod-*` does not match those requests ⚠️ | Agents can still list and describe prod. Not a write gap, but the boundary is incomplete | Use the **account boundary** as the primary layer: `nonprod` and `prod` are separate AWS accounts (OUs), GCP projects/folders, and k0s clusters. An SCP on the prod OU denies human/agent roles. Keep name deny as a **second layer** for the single-account phase |
| **G2** | **Resources with generated IDs** escape name matching: EC2 `i-…`, SG `sg-…`, KMS key UUID, ECS task IDs, ENIs, EBS volumes | A deny on `prod-*` doesn't protect them | Add **tag-based deny**: `aws:ResourceTag/env = prod`, and `aws:RequestTag/env = prod` for creation. Enforce `env` tags and naming with CrossGuard (`mandatory`) and an SCP that rejects resource creation missing an `env` tag where supported |
| **G3** | **Naming is a convention, not a guarantee.** `production-claims`, `claims-prod` or legacy resources fall outside the rule | A false sense of safety | Policy-as-code validates names in the PR. Inventory existing resources in Phase 0 and rename or tag them. A SecOps rule alerts on resources created in the prod account that don't match the convention |
| **G4** | **"Deny every action" has to exclude the pipeline and runtime roles.** Lambda/ECS roles must read `/prod/...` SSM and secrets, and the deploy role must write | Without this the deny breaks prod | Attach the deny only to **human/agent permission sets** (Identity Center), or in the SCP use `aws:PrincipalArn` to target only `AWSReservedSSO_*` roles. Pipeline and runtime roles are not affected |
| **G5** | **The debug exception has to be read-only.** If it allows writes (restart, scale, redrive), a detective control alone **fails Compliance**: the change happens before anyone reviews it | This is the most important point | Split the exception: **`prod-debug` = read-only** (detective control is enough), and **any write action = `prod-operator` through JIT with an approver** (preventive) |
| **G6** | **Telemetry is only useful with attribution and response.** A CloudTrail log saying `AWSReservedSSO_prod-debug_…` doesn't show which engineer, which agent, or which ticket. An alert nobody handles is not a control | Detective controls must be **attributable + monitored + acted on** to count as a control in an audit | Use **SourceIdentity** (engineer) and a separate role for agents. The debug session requires a **justification/ticket**. SecOps rules route to SOAR (Slack + Linear), with a response SLA, plus a **weekly review** of debug sessions (Google's break-glass review pattern) |
| **G7** | **Read-only on prod still exposes secrets and PHI**: Lambda env vars, ECS task definitions, SSM SecureString, log groups containing document content | A read-only agent can still pull PHI or secrets into the model context | `prod-debug` uses a **custom read-only policy**: deny `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`, `ssm:GetParameter*` on SecureString, `kms:Decrypt`, `s3:GetObject` on PHI buckets. Log groups with PHI are kept separate (`/prod/<service>/phi/...`) and denied |
| **G8** | **Nonprod is only safe if it holds no real PHI.** Agents get broad rights in nonprod, so production data copied into staging gives an agent all three of [A], [B] and [C] | HIPAA plus Rule of Two | Policy: **nonprod uses only synthetic or de-identified data**. Detect it: S3/Aurora snapshot copies or shares from prod to nonprod trigger a high-severity alert |

### 2.4 Verdict

**The proposal is sound and I adopt it as the backbone of v3,** with 4 required refinements:

1. **The account/project/cluster boundary is the primary layer.** Name deny + tag deny is defense-in-depth.
2. **The debug exception is read-only**, and any write goes through JIT with an approver.
3. **Telemetry carries identity** (SourceIdentity, a separate agent role, a ticket) and **ends in a response** (SOAR + weekly review).
4. **Nonprod holds no real PHI.**

## 3. Top 3 solutions for Papaya (v3)

### 3.1 Access model with 2 environments (shared by all solutions)

| Role | Env | Principal | Rights | Activation | Control type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nonprod-developer` | nonprod | Human + agent | Broad, except org/IAM-admin/billing; no real PHI | Standing | Preventive (SCP guardrails) |
| `prod-debug` | prod | Human + agent | **Custom read-only**: metrics, non-PHI logs, describe; no secrets/PHI/decrypt | **Self-service JIT 1h**, required justification + ticket (TEAM eligibility with "Approval required" off) | **Detective** (SecOps) |
| `prod-operator` | prod | Human; agent only to run a named runbook in a **new session** | Runbook actions: restart, scale, redrive DLQ, rollout restart; secret value writes (humans only, scoped by ARN) | JIT 1h, **1 approver ≠ requester** | Preventive + detective |
| `prod-breakglass` | prod | Human only | Admin, PHI reads | JIT 1h, **2 approvers**, alert to security channel, mandatory postmortem | Preventive + detective + review |
| `pipeline-deploy-prod` | prod | GitHub Actions (OIDC/WIF) | Deploy IaC/app | GitHub Environment `production` approval | Preventive |
| Runtime roles | prod | Lambda/ECS/k0s workloads | Read `/prod/<service>/*` for their own service | Not human | Least privilege per service |

**Agents and the Rule of Two:**
- In `prod-debug` the agent may read logs, which is [A] untrusted input and possibly [B] sensitive data. It has **no [C]**: no write role, and sandbox egress is limited to the cloud APIs and the model endpoint.
- To act on what it found, the agent opens a new session with `prod-operator` (after approval) to run a runbook, or goes back to a PR.

**Illustrative IAM: the deny layer** attached to human and agent permission sets (when nonprod and prod still share an account). Once accounts are split, the SCP on the prod OU takes over the main role.

### 🥇 Solution 1 — "Agent proposes, Pipeline disposes" + an observable debug exception

**Combines:** Model 4 (GitOps/PaC), Model 2 (OIDC, read-only default), Model 5 (Claude Code baseline), Model 3 (no self-escalation), plus §4 (SecOps).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Laptop["Engineer laptop · Claude Code (managed settings)"]
    A[Agent writes IaC / code] --> B[pulumi preview<br/>against nonprod]
  end
  Laptop -- nonprod-developer --> NP[(nonprod accounts/projects/cluster)]
  Laptop -. prod-debug: self-service JIT, read-only,<br/>SourceIdentity + ticket .-> P[(prod)]
  B --> PR[PR in monorepo]
  PR --> CI[CI: tests, SAST, secret scan,<br/>naming/tag policy, CrossGuard,<br/>sls package + CFN change-set diff]
  CI --> R{CODEOWNERS review<br/>approver ≠ last pusher}
  R -->|merge| ENV{Environment 'production'<br/>required reviewer,<br/>prevent self-review}
  ENV -->|OIDC / WIF| DEP[pulumi up · sls deploy ·<br/>Argo CD sync · firebase deploy]
  DEP --> P
  P -. CloudTrail / GCP Audit / k0s audit .-> SIEM[(Google SecOps)]
  Laptop -. Claude Code OTel .-> SIEM
  ENV -. GitHub audit: approver .-> SIEM
```

**How it works**

1. **Two environments, isolated by account/project/cluster, plus naming/tag deny** (§3.1). Engineers and agents have broad rights in nonprod and **no write path** to prod.
2. **The only road for prod changes** (unchanged from v2):
   - The PR runs `pulumi preview` against prod and CrossGuard `mandatory`. Don't use `remediate` on prod.
   - For Serverless, run `serverless package` and post the CFN change-set diff on the PR.
   - CODEOWNERS + ruleset "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push".
   - Environment `production` with Prevent self-review.
   - Deploy through OIDC (AWS) or WIF (GCP, Firebase). Remove every long-lived key and PAT.
3. **New in v3: policy-as-code checks naming and tags.** Every resource in a prod stack must have a name that starts with `prod-` (SSM: `/prod/`) and the tags `env=prod`, `service`, `owner`, `data-class`. This closes G2 and G3.
4. **The debug exception (`prod-debug`):**
   - **Activation:** the engineer activates it themselves through TEAM. Approval is off, but a justification and Linear ticket are required, and the TTL is 1h. The engineer's username is set as **SourceIdentity** ⚠️.
   - **Agent sessions:** agents use a separate profile and role, `prod-debug-agent`, with the same rights. CloudTrail can then separate agents from humans without depending on the AWS MCP condition keys.
   - **Permissions:** custom read-only (G7). No secrets, PHI or decrypt.
   - **Telemetry:** every API call goes to Google SecOps (§4), with rules and a weekly review.
5. **Config and secrets** (from v2.1, adapted to the naming convention):
   - Config and secret **definitions** live in git under `/<env>/<service>/<name>`. Secret **values** live in Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager and **never pass through the agent's context**.
   - Machine secrets rotate automatically (RDS managed master password). Third-party secrets are entered by a human through `prod-operator` (scoped by ARN, approver ≠ requester).
   - Applications read secrets at runtime (ECS `secrets`, the Lambda extension, External Secrets Operator on k0s). Don't use Serverless `${ssm:}` for secrets, because it resolves into plaintext at deploy time ⚠️.
   - CloudTrail alerts on `PutSecretValue`/`PutParameter` against `/prod/*` that don't come from the pipeline or `prod-operator`.
6. **Claude Code managed baseline:** keys verified against the docs on 2026-11-05.

**Why #1**
- It keeps the simplicity of the 2-environment model.
- It satisfies both quotes. Every prod change has a named approver in GitHub, and Engineering gets to debug prod without waiting.
- It closes risks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (with §4) and 7 (NoPHI by default).
- It reuses existing tooling, apart from SecOps.

### 🥈 Solution 2 — S1 + JIT for prod actions (`prod-operator`, `prod-breakglass`) — **90-day target**

**Combines:** Model 2 (JIT), Model 1 (MPA, break-glass), Model 3 (PIM-style approval), Model 5 (Rule of Two).

**What it adds:** a *preventive* path for prod writes that can't go through a PR (incidents, runbooks, entering third-party secrets), in line with refinement G5.

1. **`prod-operator`:**
   - A whitelist of runbook actions, 1h TTL, 1 approver ≠ requester, and a ticket.
   - If Compliance accepts *approval-by-policy*, then on-call with an open incident can be auto-approved. That requires a broker with conditional approval.
   - Agents may only use it to **run a named runbook in a new session**.
2. **`prod-breakglass`:**
   - 2 approvers (MPA), an alert to the security channel, a mandatory postmortem, and a quarterly test.
   - It directly meets HIPAA 164.312(a)(2)(ii) *Emergency access procedure* (Required).
3. **Broker:**
   - **AWS TEAM:** free and AWS-native. Approval is web-app only, and it has no conditional auto-approval. It fits `prod-debug` (approval off) and `prod-operator`/`prod-breakglass` (approval on).
   - **Common Fate/Granted or Teleport:** if Slack approval, conditional auto-approval, or coverage of k0s and GCP is needed. ⚠️ Pricing.
4. **Agents can't escalate:** an SCP/permission boundary denies `iam:*`, `organizations:*`, `sso:*`, `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion`, `rds:DeleteDBCluster`, and `s3:DeleteBucket` to `prod-debug-agent` and to agent sessions.
5. **HIPAA gate:**
   - Anthropic's BAA covers Claude Code on **Enterprise + HIPAA configuration**. The Team plan is not addressed.
   - Bedrock/Vertex fall outside Anthropic's BAA. Bedrock coverage comes from the AWS BAA ⚠️.
   - Until Legal decides, **agents never read PHI**, so `prod-breakglass` is humans only.

**Trade-offs**
| Gain | Cost |
|---|---|
| Writes on prod during incidents stay fast and have an approver | +6 weeks; policy is easy to get wrong (`prod-operator` too broad turns into admin) |
| Time-boxed, attributable | TEAM has no approve-in-Slack; upgrading the broker costs money |
| Break-glass meets a HIPAA Required spec | Changes made by `prod-operator` aren't in git, so they need reconciliation (a follow-up PR or a revert), and SecOps tracks the drift |

### 🥉 Solution 3 — Centralized Agent Runtime: agents run on managed infrastructure, laptops hold no cloud credentials

**Combines:** Model 5 (Copilot-coding-agent-style sandbox), Model 1 (agent = workload identity), Model 3 (dedicated agent identity).

- **Where agents run:** infra-capable agent tasks run on ephemeral runners (GitHub Actions + Claude Code Action, or devcontainers on EC2/k0s), each with its own agent identity per task type and environment (OIDC/WIF).
- **Laptops hold no cloud credentials.**
- **Runner controls:** firewalled egress, credentials TTL 15–60 minutes, transcripts in S3 Object Lock and sent to SecOps, and MCP from a curated image.
- **Prompt injection in CI:**
  - Never combine `pull_request_target` with a PR-head checkout.
  - Only writers can trigger the agent.
  - An agent job that reads untrusted content gets a read-only token and no prod credentials, and its output is a PR.
- **Why #3:** it is the most secure but the most expensive (3–6 months), it slows the debug loop, and without S1/S2 it invites "shadow agents". It is the **18-month direction** for background tasks (drift remediation, dependency upgrades).

| Gain | Cost |
|---|---|
| No credentials on laptops | Highest effort plus an ops team |
| Complete, immutable transcripts | Interactive debugging is slower |
| Easy to apply Rule of Two per job type | Runners become high-value targets; the CI attack surface grows |
